name: Design Live Comments and Reactions
intent: Let millions of people watching one live stream post comments and tap reactions, and show everyone a lively, readable, moderated feed and a reaction count within a second or two.
codeTitle: edge aggregation and mergeable sampling of live events
finalIntro: One comment and one burst of reactions travelling through the finished design.
prompt: Design the live comments and reactions for a live stream with 5 million concurrent viewers. Viewers post comments and tap hearts, laughs and claps. Everyone should see the same lively comment feed and floating reactions about a second behind the event, with abusive comments filtered out.
functional: Post a comment on the stream
Send a reaction (heart, laugh, clap, wow) with a tap
See a live feed of comments, in a sensible order
See the reactions as a live animation and a running count
Block abusive comments and ban abusive users quickly
Catch up on recent comments after joining late or reconnecting
nonFunctional: A comment or reaction appears for other viewers within about 2 seconds
Handle tens of thousands of reactions and thousands of comments per second at the peak
Hold millions of open connections without one slow viewer harming the others
Each viewer reads a small, steady stream, not every event
Reaction counts may be approximate, but a counted reaction is never shown twice
A flash crowd at a goal or an announcement must not take the service down

firstAttempt.text: One chat server holds every viewer's WebSocket. A comment is inserted in a database and then written to every connection in a loop, and each reaction is a message to every connection too.
limits: One server cannot hold millions of connections, and one loop cannot write to all of them in a second
Sending every comment to every viewer is millions of times the data: 2,778 comments per second times 5 million viewers is about 2.8 TB every second
No phone can read thousands of comments per second, so most of what is sent is wasted
One slow viewer fills the buffer on the server, and the loop stalls or runs out of memory
Fifty thousand reaction writes per second to a database serve no purpose, since a count is all anyone needs
An abusive comment has already reached everyone by the time anyone looks at it

steps.title: Hold connections in a gateway tier and split writes from reads
steps.problem: A single server cannot hold millions of open connections, and a viewer's connection should not be tied to the machine that stores comments.
steps.fix: A fleet of connection gateways holds the WebSockets, about 50,000 each, so 5 million viewers need about 100 gateways behind a load balancer. A gateway does no business logic. It passes a posted comment to a separate ingest service, which authenticates, rate-limits per user, and appends the comment to a durable log with an id and a timestamp. Connections and storage now scale on their own.
steps.tradeoff: Each part scales on its own and a gateway can be replaced without losing comments, because the log holds them. There is one more hop for every comment, and a deploy that restarts a gateway makes 50,000 phones reconnect at once, so reconnects need jitter.

steps.title: Count reactions in tiers instead of storing them
steps.problem: Reactions are 50,000 taps per second, they are all the same kind of event, and nobody needs any single tap. Writing and forwarding each one is pure waste.
steps.fix: Each gateway keeps four counters in memory, one per reaction type, and adds each tap to them. Once a second it sends one small tally to the counters service, about 500 taps folded into one message. The counters merge the tallies from all 100 gateways by adding, which gives the total for that second, and a running total. Adding is commutative, so the order of arrival does not matter and a late tally just adds in.
steps.tradeoff: Fifty thousand events per second become 100 messages per second, and the work does not grow with viewers. A gateway that crashes loses up to a second of taps, which is acceptable for reactions, and a tally resent after a retry must carry an id so it is not added twice.

steps.title: Fan out through pub/sub tiers
steps.problem: Sending a message to 5 million viewers from one place needs millions of writes, which no single publisher can do in a second.
steps.fix: The stream has one pub/sub topic. Comments and tallies are published once, and the topic feeds a relay tier. Each relay serves about 10 gateways, and each gateway writes to its own 50,000 connections. Fan-out is a tree: 1 topic, 10 relays, 100 gateways, 5 million phones, with each level sending only to the level below. A gateway subscribes to the stream topics its viewers watch and nothing else.
steps.tradeoff: No machine has to write more than about 50,000 times per message, and adding viewers adds gateways, not load on the root. Every tier adds a little latency, about tens of milliseconds, and a message can be lost between tiers, so each message carries a sequence number that lets a gateway notice a gap and fetch the missing part.

steps.title: Sample the comments so the feed is readable
steps.problem: At 2,778 comments per second nobody can read the feed, and sending every comment to 5 million viewers would be about 2.8 TB per second.
steps.fix: A sampler picks at most about 10 comments per second for the whole stream, and every viewer gets the same ones. Each comment gets a priority from a fixed hash of its id, perhaps boosted for subscribers, moderators or replies, and the sampler keeps the highest few in each second. Because the priority is a function of the comment alone, partial samplers can each keep their best few and merge their lists. Ordering is by second, then by priority, and sequence numbers let gateways replay in order.
steps.tradeoff: Egress drops by a factor of hundreds, and the feed looks the same for everyone, which makes it feel shared. Most comments are never shown, so the writer should be told they were received, and a fair priority rule matters, since it decides whose voice is heard.

steps.title: Moderate before comments reach the crowd
steps.problem: One abusive comment shown to 5 million viewers is a brand and legal problem, and a human cannot review thousands per second.
steps.fix: Every comment passes through moderation before it is eligible for sampling. Fast checks run inline: a blocklist, a link and spam filter, a per-user rate limit, and a machine-learning score for toxicity. A comment that is clearly fine goes on, one that is clearly bad is dropped, and the uncertain ones are held for human review. Comments are shown as plain text and escaped, so a comment cannot run code in other viewers' apps. Banning a user takes effect at the ingest tier within seconds.
steps.tradeoff: Harm is stopped before it reaches the crowd, and since most comments are never shown, only the few that win the sampling need the expensive check. Inline checks add tens of milliseconds, classifiers make mistakes in both directions, and a late ban cannot unsend a comment, which is why a delete message can also be published to remove it from open screens.

steps.title: Protect gateways from slow clients and catch up on reconnect
steps.problem: A phone on a poor network reads slowly, and its unsent messages pile up in the gateway's memory. A thousand such phones can crash the gateway and take down 50,000 healthy viewers.
steps.fix: Every connection has a small bounded queue. When it fills, the gateway drops the oldest comments but never the newest tally, and it sends a slow client fewer comments, matched to what it can read. A client that stays behind is disconnected. When a phone joins or reconnects it asks for the recent comments from a small cache, using the last sequence number it saw, so catching up never goes through the live path. Reconnects use random delays so a restart is not followed by a stampede.
steps.tradeoff: Memory per gateway is bounded and slow viewers cannot hurt the rest. Slow viewers see a thinner and older feed, and a reconnect storm still loads the cache, which is why it is cached and rate-limited.

failures.scenario: A goal is scored and reactions jump from 50,000 to 500,000 per second
failures.impact: Gateways receive ten times the taps, and counters and relays could be overloaded.
failures.answer: Gateways fold taps into counters in memory, so the messages upstream are the same 100 tallies per second whatever the taps. Each gateway also caps taps per connection per second, and the phone animation shows a number scaled from the tally, not one animation per tap.

failures.scenario: A relay or a gateway crashes
failures.impact: Up to 50,000 viewers stop receiving the feed and all reconnect at the same moment.
failures.answer: Health checks remove the node, and phones reconnect to another gateway with randomised backoff. On reconnect the phone sends its last sequence number and receives the missing comments from the recent cache. Gateways are stateless apart from their queues, so any gateway can take over.

failures.impact: Without a limit, memory grows until the gateway is killed and its 50,000 viewers all lose the stream.
failures.answer: Each queue is bounded. When it fills the oldest comments are dropped, the client is sampled down to its own speed, and a client that keeps falling behind is disconnected and sent to the catch-up path.

failures.scenario: A spam wave of bot accounts posts thousands of comments per second
failures.impact: The ingest tier is busy and the sample could fill with spam.
failures.answer: Per-user and per-address rate limits and new-account limits drop most of it at the gateway. The sampler boosts accounts with good history, and moderation scores the rest. A global limit on ingest protects the log if the attack is large.

failures.scenario: The pub/sub topic or a relay drops a message
failures.impact: Some viewers miss a comment or a tally, and the feeds of two viewers differ.
failures.answer: Messages carry a sequence number per stream. A gateway that sees a gap asks the recent-comments cache for the missing range. Reaction tallies are absolute totals per second, so the next tally corrects the count and nothing needs replay.

alternatives.title: How to deliver to phones

options.name: WebSockets or server-sent events through gateways
options.pro: Low delay, and the server can push
options.con: Millions of open connections to hold and to rebalance

options.name: Short polling of a cached feed
options.pro: Stateless, and the CDN can serve it
options.con: Delay equals the polling interval, and the load is constant

options.name: A CDN-delivered feed file refreshed every second or two
options.pro: Scales to any number of viewers cheaply
options.con: Latency of two or three seconds, and no per-viewer reactions

alternatives.pick: Gateways with WebSockets for interactive streams. Feed files from a CDN for the very largest audiences where a few seconds of delay is fine.

alternatives.title: How to handle reactions

options.name: Send each reaction to everyone
options.con: Millions of times the traffic and no phone can draw it

options.name: Count in tiers and publish one tally per second
options.con: A counted tap is anonymous and a second late

alternatives.pick: Count in tiers. Sampling only for the largest streams.

alternatives.title: How to choose which comments are shown

options.name: Newest first, all of them
options.con: Unreadable at thousands per second, and bursts move the whole feed

options.name: Random sample by hash
options.pro: Same for every viewer, and mergeable across nodes

options.name: Ranked by a quality or engagement score
options.con: Needs a score, and a delay for it to build up

alternatives.pick: Hash sampling with small boosts for verified, subscriber and reply comments.

alternatives.title: Where moderation runs

options.name: After display, with reports
options.con: The harm has already reached millions

options.name: Before sampling, inline
options.con: Adds latency and cost per comment

options.name: Only on the sampled few
options.con: A comment must be checked before it is promoted, which adds a step

alternatives.pick: Cheap filters on every comment, and the expensive check on the few that win the sampling.
